Wrong, a reactive NST does not mandate delivery
exp: A reactive NST at 32 weeks or beyond requires 2 or more accelerations of at least 15 bpm above baseline lasting at least 15 seconds within a 20-minute window; the tracing described meets and exceeds this criterion, so it is reactive and reassuring.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 32-year-old woman with 6 months of amenorrhea and hot flashes has FSH of 42 IU/L on two occasions 6 weeks apart, with normal prolactin and TSH. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Wrong, PCOS has normal or low FSH with a high LH to FSH ratio
Wrong, hypothalamic amenorrhea has LOW FSH and LH, not elevated
Correct, elevated FSH x2 with hypoestrogenic symptoms confirms POI
Wrong, Asherman has normal FSH with intrauterine adhesions on hysteroscopy
exp: Premature ovarian insufficiency is defined as amenorrhea for 4 months or more with menopausal-range FSH on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart in a woman under 40; hypoestrogenic symptoms with normal prolactin and TSH excluding other causes confirms POI, warranting karyotype and FMR1 premutation testing plus hormone replacement for bone and cardiovascular protection.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 28-year-old woman with migraine with aura wants to start combined oral contraceptive pills. What is the most appropriate advice regarding cardiovascular risk?
opts: Combined OCPs are safe and first-line
Only progestin-only pills need to be avoided
Combined OCPs are safe if she is under 35 years old
Combined OCPs are contraindicated due to increased stroke risk
why: Wrong, not safe in this scenario
Wrong, the reverse is true, progestin-only is the safe alternative
Wrong, age does not offset the aura-related stroke risk
Correct, WHO MEC category 4, unacceptable risk
exp: Per WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria, combined hormonal contraceptives are Category 4 in women with migraine with aura at any age, due to a significantly increased risk of ischemic stroke from the estrogen component; progestin-only methods are safe alternatives.

subject: OBGYN
q: Under the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021 in India, termination of pregnancy up to 24 weeks of gestation is permitted only for which category of women, and requires the opinion of how many registered medical practitioners?
opts: Special categories (survivors of rape or incest, minors, women with fetal abnormality, etc.); two RMP opinions
Any married woman; one RMP opinion
Any woman on request; two RMP opinions
Special categories only; no RMP opinion required, self-certification suffices
why: Correct, extended limit applies only to special categories with two RMP opinions
Wrong, not any married woman, and up to 20 weeks needs only one RMP
Wrong, not available on request beyond 20 weeks
Wrong, two RMP opinions are mandatory, self-certification is insufficient
exp: The MTP Amendment Act 2021 extended the upper gestational limit from 20 to 24 weeks only for specific categories such as survivors of sexual assault, minors, and cases of fetal malformation incompatible with life, and mandates the opinion of two registered medical practitioners versus one RMP for termination up to 20 weeks.

subject: OBGYN
q: A sexually active woman presents with frothy, greenish-yellow malodorous vaginal discharge and vulvar itching. Speculum examination reveals a strawberry cervix with punctate haemorrhages. Wet mount microscopy is most likely to show which finding?
why: Wrong, clue cells indicate bacterial vaginosis
Correct, motile flagellated trichomonads on wet mount
Wrong, candidiasis gives curdy discharge with pseudohyphae
Wrong, gonorrhoea is diagnosed by culture or NAAT, not wet mount
exp: Trichomonas vaginalis produces frothy greenish discharge, malodour, and the classic strawberry cervix from punctate submucosal haemorrhages; wet mount shows motile, flagellated, pear-shaped trichomonads. Treat with oral metronidazole or tinidazole for the patient and her partner, since it is an STI.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 36 weeks develops sudden painless vaginal bleeding immediately after spontaneous rupture of membranes, accompanied by acute fetal bradycardia on cardiotocography, with the mother remaining hemodynamically stable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Wrong, abruption is typically painful with uterine tenderness
Wrong, previa bleeding is not classically precipitated by ROM with immediate fetal bradycardia
Correct, fetal vessel rupture at ROM causes painless bleeding with fetal distress and stable mother
Wrong, rupture typically occurs in labour with a scarred uterus and maternal shock
exp: Vasa previa involves fetal vessels running unprotected across the internal os; rupture of membranes tears these vessels causing painless bleeding of fetal origin, so a small blood loss causes disproportionate fetal distress while the mother stays stable. Confirm with an Apt test if time permits; management is emergency caesarean.

subject: OBGYN
q: A couple undergoing infertility workup has an HSG showing a right-sided dilated, sausage-shaped fallopian tube with pooling of contrast and no peritoneal spillage. Before proceeding with IVF, what should be done to improve pregnancy success rates?
opts: No intervention needed, proceed directly to IVF
Bilateral salpingectomy regardless of the contralateral tube
Repeat HSG in 3 months to reassess
Salpingectomy or proximal tubal occlusion of the affected tube
why: Wrong, untreated hydrosalpinx lowers IVF success rates
Wrong, only the diseased tube needs treatment, not necessarily bilateral
Wrong, delay without treatment doesn't address the embryotoxic effect
Correct, treating the affected tube before IVF improves implantation rates
exp: A hydrosalpinx reduces IVF success because hydrosalpingeal fluid is embryotoxic and can reflux into the endometrial cavity, impairing implantation; laparoscopic salpingectomy or proximal tubal occlusion of the affected tube before IVF significantly improves implantation and live-birth rates.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman practicing a fertility awareness method notices her cervical mucus become clear, thin, and stretchy, forming a thread when pulled between two fingers, around day 13 of her cycle. This finding indicates she is closest to which physiological event?
why: Correct, Spinnbarkeit mucus signals the fertile window before ovulation
Wrong, menstrual mucus is absent or scant
Wrong, implantation occurs 6 to 10 days post-ovulation when mucus has already thickened under progesterone
Wrong, luteolysis is late-cycle, mucus is thick and scant then
exp: Rising estrogen just before the LH surge causes cervical mucus to become thin, clear, and elastic with ferning on microscopy, creating a sperm-friendly channel; this mucus change signals the fertile window immediately preceding ovulation, the physiological basis of the Billings fertility awareness method.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 32 weeks with reduced fetal movements undergoes ultrasound showing an amniotic fluid index of 4 cm. How should this finding be classified and what is an important next step?
opts: Normal AFI; reassure and routine follow-up
Oligohydramnios; evaluate for causes such as PPROM, fetal renal or growth anomalies, placental insufficiency, and increase surveillance
why: Wrong, 4 cm is below the normal AFI range
Correct, AFI under 5 cm defines oligohydramnios needing workup
Wrong, opposite finding
Wrong, this is an actionable finding now, not a wait and recheck value
exp: Amniotic fluid index under 5 cm defines oligohydramnios; causes include ruptured membranes, uteroplacental insufficiency or growth restriction, and fetal renal anomalies. It warrants prompt workup and increased antenatal surveillance given the association with adverse perinatal outcomes including cord compression.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 16-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea, absent breast development, and an inability to smell coffee or perfume on testing. Serum FSH and LH are both low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Wrong, Turner has elevated, not low, FSH and LH from primary ovarian failure, plus short stature, no anosmia
Wrong, AIS has normal breast development and absent uterus with normal or high testosterone, no anosmia
Correct, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism plus anosmia is classic for Kallmann syndrome
Wrong, PCOS doesn't cause primary amenorrhea with absent puberty or low gonadotropins
exp: Kallmann syndrome results from failed migration of GnRH-secreting neurons, which co-migrate embryologically with olfactory neurons, causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with low FSH and LH, low estrogen, and absent puberty, classically combined with anosmia or hyposmia.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman who had massive postpartum haemorrhage requiring blood transfusion during delivery fails to lactate and has persistent amenorrhea 3 months postpartum, along with fatigue and cold intolerance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Wrong, doesn't explain failed lactation as the presenting picture
Wrong, assumes ongoing lactation, but lactation itself failed here
Wrong, doesn't explain failed lactation or hypothyroid features
Correct, postpartum pituitary necrosis after severe PPH explains failed lactation and panhypopituitarism
exp: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum pituitary necrosis following severe obstetric haemorrhage and hypotension, since the physiologically hyperplastic pituitary of pregnancy is vulnerable to ischemic infarction without a proportionate increase in blood supply. Failure of lactation is often the earliest clue, followed by amenorrhea and features of panhypopituitarism.

subject: OBGYN
q: In a woman with postpartum haemorrhage, tranexamic acid reduces death due to bleeding when given within what time window after delivery?
why: Correct — the WOMAN trial showed mortality benefit only within this window
Too late — no mortality benefit demonstrated at this window
Unnecessarily narrow — not the studied cutoff
Too late — no mortality benefit demonstrated at this window
exp: The WOMAN trial (Lancet 2017) showed IV tranexamic acid 1g given within 3 hours of delivery significantly reduced death due to bleeding in PPH, with no benefit shown for later administration — it is now recommended by WHO as an adjunct to uterotonics in all PPH cases.

subject: OBGYN
q: As part of active management of the third stage of labour, prophylactic oxytocin is administered at what point?
opts: Before delivery of the placenta, after waiting 30 minutes
Immediately after delivery of the placenta
At the onset of the second stage of labour
Within 1 minute of delivery of the baby, before delivery of the placenta
why: Delayed administration blunts the preventive effect
Too late — the point is prophylaxis before the placenta separates
Premature — it is given after birth of the baby, not before
Correct — this is the WHO-recommended AMTSL timing
exp: WHO-recommended active management of the third stage (AMTSL) is oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV within 1 minute of the baby's birth, followed by controlled cord traction — this markedly reduces the incidence of PPH and is standard practice for every vaginal delivery.

subject: OBGYN
q: During hysterectomy, the uterine artery crosses over a structure that is at particular risk of injury during ligation of the uterine vessels. Which structure is this?
why: The round ligament is divided early and is not at this crossing point
Ovarian vessels run in the infundibulopelvic ligament, a separate site
Correct — the uterine artery crosses anterior/superior to the ureter, ('water under the bridge')
The obturator nerve lies in the obturator fossa, relevant to pelvic lymphadenectomy, not uterine artery ligation
exp: The uterine artery passes anterior and superior to the ureter roughly 1.5-2 cm lateral to the cervix, a relationship every operating surgeon must identify to avoid ureteric injury during hysterectomy or any pelvic surgery near the cervix.

subject: OBGYN
q: A primiparous woman on postpartum day 4, exclusively breastfeeding, develops fever of 38.6C with a tender, warm, wedge-shaped area of erythema on one breast but no fluctuant mass. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Stop breastfeeding on the affected side until it resolves
Continue breastfeeding/pumping and start antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus
Reassurance only, as this is physiological engorgement
why: Stopping feeding worsens milk stasis and raises abscess risk
Correct — continued drainage plus an anti-staphylococcal antibiotic is first-line for mastitis
No fluctuant mass is described, so this is not yet an abscess
Fever and focal wedge-shaped erythema rule out simple bilateral engorgement
exp: Puerperal mastitis is unilateral, febrile, and wedge-shaped, distinguishing it from bilateral afebrile engorgement and from a frank abscess (fluctuant, needs drainage); management is continued milk drainage plus an anti-staphylococcal antibiotic such as dicloxacillin or cephalexin, since stopping feeding raises abscess risk.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 28-year-old woman reports secondary amenorrhea for 6 months with bilateral milky nipple discharge. TSH is normal, urine pregnancy test is negative, and visual fields are full. Serum prolactin is 120 ng/mL. What is the most likely underlying cause?
why: Correct — a markedly elevated prolactin with normal TSH points to a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma
Hypothyroidism raises prolactin only mildly via TRH stimulation, and TSH here is normal
Physiological/stress causes typically elevate prolactin only modestly (usually under 50 ng/mL)
PCOS causes anovulation but not galactorrhea or this degree of hyperprolactinemia
exp: A markedly elevated prolactin (well above 100 ng/mL) with a normal TSH and negative pregnancy test strongly suggests a prolactin-secreting pituitary microadenoma; the next step is pituitary MRI, and first-line treatment is a dopamine agonist (cabergoline) rather than surgery in most cases.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman with obesity (BMI 33) and type 2 diabetes presents with a single episode of vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 14 mm. Which diagnosis is most strongly suggested by her risk profile?
why: Polyps are a common benign cause of AUB but carry no specific link to this metabolic risk profile
Leiomyomas are a common benign cause of AUB but carry no specific link to this metabolic risk profile
Cervical ectropion causes contact spotting, not endometrial thickening
Correct — obesity and diabetes reflect chronic unopposed estrogen, the classic endometrioid carcinoma risk profile
exp: Obesity and diabetes reflect a state of chronic unopposed peripheral estrogen (from aromatization of androgens in adipose tissue) without progesterone opposition, the classic metabolic risk triad for endometrioid-type endometrial carcinoma; any postmenopausal bleeding with a thickened endometrium mandates biopsy before assuming a benign cause.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 6 weeks by LMP has minimal spotting with a closed cervical os. Quantitative beta-hCG is 1500 mIU/mL, and transvaginal ultrasound shows no intrauterine gestational sac and no adnexal mass. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Immediate laparoscopy for suspected ectopic pregnancy
Diagnose missed abortion and start misoprostol
Repeat quantitative beta-hCG in 48 hours to assess the trend
Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
why: Too aggressive without a confirmed ectopic location
No ultrasound evidence yet of a failed intrauterine pregnancy
Correct — a pregnancy of unknown location near the discriminatory zone needs a serial hCG trend before acting
Unsafe given the real possibility of ectopic pregnancy; close follow-up is required
exp: This is a pregnancy of unknown location: beta-hCG near the discriminatory zone (~1500-2000 mIU/mL) without a visible intrauterine or adnexal pregnancy requires serial beta-hCG measurement (a viable intrauterine pregnancy roughly doubles every 48 hours) rather than immediate intervention, since acting too early risks disrupting a viable pregnancy.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 34 weeks gestation with known preeclampsia develops severe epigastric pain. Labs show platelets 68,000/microL, AST 180 U/L, ALT 165 U/L, and schistocytes on peripheral smear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: AFLP typically shows hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, and markedly deranged liver function without this hemolysis pattern
Correct — hemolysis (schistocytes), elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets define HELLP as a severe preeclampsia variant
Cholecystitis does not explain thrombocytopenia or hemolysis
Septic DIC would have accompanying clinical evidence of infection/fever
exp: HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) is a severe variant of preeclampsia; schistocytes confirm microangiopathic hemolysis and epigastric/RUQ pain reflects hepatic capsule distension from periportal necrosis; definitive management is delivery once the mother is stabilized, regardless of gestational age.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman with two prior cesarean deliveries has an anterior placenta previa at 32 weeks. Ultrasound shows loss of the normal retroplacental clear space, multiple vascular lacunae (Swiss cheese appearance), and irregularity of the bladder wall-uterine interface. What is the most likely diagnosis and its recommended management?
opts: Placenta accreta spectrum; planned cesarean hysterectomy at a tertiary centre
Placenta previa alone; vaginal delivery is safe if bleeding is controlled
Vasa previa; elective cesarean at 36-37 weeks without further imaging
Marginal previa; expectant management until spontaneous labour
why: Correct — the sonographic triad plus prior cesarean and previa is classic for placenta accreta spectrum, needing a planned hysterectomy at a well-resourced centre
Ignores the accreta features and the absolute contraindication to vaginal delivery in previa
Vasa previa has a distinct sonographic signature (vessels crossing the internal os on colour Doppler), not described here
The described findings are far beyond a simple marginal previa
exp: Loss of the retroplacental clear space, multiple irregular lacunae, and bladder wall interruption in a woman with prior cesareans and anterior previa form the classic sonographic triad of placenta accreta spectrum; a planned, pre-scheduled cesarean hysterectomy at a centre with blood bank and interventional radiology backup minimizes the risk of catastrophic hemorrhage.

subject: OBGYN
q: A labouring woman's CTG shows repetitive, abrupt-onset decelerations coinciding with contractions, with moderate baseline variability maintained between episodes. What is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Administer terbutaline for suspected uterine hyperstimulation
Change maternal position and consider amnioinfusion
why: Premature — preserved variability argues against significant acidosis needing immediate delivery
Augmentation would increase contraction frequency and worsen cord compression
Terbutaline treats uterine tachysystole/hyperstimulation, not the pattern described here
Correct — abrupt variable decelerations with preserved variability suggest cord compression, managed by position change +/- amnioinfusion
exp: Abrupt, variable-shaped decelerations with preserved baseline variability are typical of umbilical cord compression rather than fetal acidosis; first-line management is a maternal position change with amnioinfusion considered if oligohydramnios or persistent compression is present, since preserved variability is reassuring.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 13-year-old girl who has already started menstruating presents with progressively worsening cyclical pelvic pain despite apparently normal menstrual flow. Examination reveals a bulging vaginal mass, and imaging shows a uterus didelphys with an obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal agenesis. What is this syndrome called?
opts: OHVIRA (obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal anomaly) syndrome
why: MRKH is absent uterus/vagina with normal ovaries, not a didelphys uterus with obstruction
AIS is 46,XY with absent uterus and a blind vaginal pouch
Correct — uterus didelphys plus obstructed hemivagina plus ipsilateral renal agenesis defines OHVIRA
Asherman syndrome is acquired intrauterine adhesions, unrelated to this congenital anomaly
exp: OHVIRA results from failure of fusion/canalization of one Mullerian duct with a concurrent ipsilateral mesonephric (renal) duct anomaly, producing uterus didelphys with one obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal agenesis; it presents post-menarche with cyclical pain from hematocolpos on the obstructed side, and is treated by surgical resection of the vaginal septum.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 24-year-old woman with PCOS and 18 months of infertility has failed to conceive despite lifestyle modification. Which drug is now preferred as first-line ovulation induction agent over clomiphene citrate?
why: Metformin helps insulin resistance and is adjunctive, not a primary ovulation-inducing agent, especially in obese PCOS
Correct - letrozole gives higher ovulation and live-birth rates than clomiphene in PCOS
Gonadotropins are second-line after oral agent failure, given cost and OHSS/multiple-pregnancy risk
Bromocriptine treats hyperprolactinemia-related anovulation, not PCOS per se
exp: Letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, produces higher ovulation and live-birth rates than clomiphene citrate in PCOS-related anovulatory infertility (Legro et al., NEJM 2014) and is now favoured first-line by ESHRE/ASRM guidance, though used off-label in India.

subject: OBGYN
q: A primigravida at 32 weeks presents with sudden gush of clear fluid per vaginum, confirmed rupture of membranes, no contractions, afebrile, and reassuring fetal heart rate. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Immediate induction of labour irrespective of gestational age
Tocolysis alone without antibiotics or steroids
Expectant management with latency antibiotics and antenatal corticosteroids
why: Immediate induction is reserved for term PPROM or evidence of infection/fetal compromise.
Caesarean section is not indicated by PPROM alone without obstetric indication.
Tocolysis alone, without antibiotics or steroids, is not the standard approach in PPROM.
Correct - expectant management with latency antibiotics and a single corticosteroid course is preferred before 34 weeks without infection or fetal compromise.
exp: In PPROM before 34 weeks without chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise, expectant management is preferred: latency antibiotics prolong pregnancy and reduce infection risk, while antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturity; delivery is reserved for infection, non-reassuring status, or advancing gestation.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 41 weeks 3 days gestation with reassuring fetal heart rate and an unfavorable cervix (Bishop score 3) presents for antenatal check. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Expectant management till 42 weeks without intervention
Elective caesarean section without trial of labour
Expectant management with twice-weekly NST and amniotic fluid index till spontaneous labour
Cervical ripening followed by induction of labour
why: Unmonitored expectant management beyond 41 weeks raises stillbirth and macrosomia risk.
Caesarean section is not first-line; induction is attempted first with adequate monitoring.
Even with surveillance, continuing to await spontaneous labour past 41 weeks is not favoured over active induction by current guidance.
Correct - cervical ripening followed by induction is recommended for post-term pregnancy with an unfavorable cervix.
exp: Post-term pregnancy beyond 41 weeks with an unfavorable cervix warrants cervical ripening followed by induction, since continuing beyond 41-42 weeks raises stillbirth, macrosomia, and meconium aspiration risk; a low Bishop score is a reason to ripen first, not to withhold induction.

subject: OBGYN
q: A monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy on ultrasound shows one twin with oligohydramnios and a stuck appearance, while the co-twin shows polyhydramnios and cardiomegaly. What is the diagnosis?
why: TRAP sequence involves an acardiac twin perfused by the co-twin, a distinct entity
Conjoined twins is a structural fusion anomaly, not a fluid-volume discordance
Selective IUGR is a growth discordance without this fluid pattern
Correct - unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses cause the donor/recipient fluid pattern
exp: TTTS results from unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses in monochorionic twins - the donor twin becomes oliguric with oligohydramnios (stuck twin), the recipient becomes polyuric with polyhydramnios and volume-overload cardiomegaly; severity is graded by Quintero staging.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 32-year-old woman's Pap smear shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, and colposcopy-directed biopsy confirms CIN 2. What is the recommended next step in management?
opts: Observation only, as CIN 2 regresses spontaneously in all cases
Loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) or cold-knife conization
why: Repeat smear alone under-treats a high-grade lesion
Hysterectomy is not first-line for CIN, reserved for select recurrent or inaccessible cases
CIN 2/3 has a lower spontaneous regression rate than CIN 1 and needs active treatment
Correct - excisional treatment is indicated for CIN 2/3
exp: CIN 2/3 (high-grade lesions) with satisfactory colposcopy warrants excisional treatment - LEEP or cold-knife conization - to prevent progression to invasive cervical cancer.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 30 weeks gestation presents with regular uterine contractions and cervical dilatation of 3 cm, with intact membranes and no signs of infection. Along with corticosteroids, which agent is appropriate for short-term tocolysis?
why: Oxytocin promotes labour, the opposite of tocolysis
Misoprostol is a uterotonic used for induction/PPH, not tocolysis
Correct - nifedipine is a first-line tocolytic
Ergometrine is a uterotonic used in PPH management and is contraindicated in tocolysis
exp: Nifedipine is a first-line tocolytic used to delay preterm labour by roughly 48 hours, allowing completion of antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity and/or safe in-utero transfer.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman attempting VBAC at 39 weeks develops sudden severe suprapubic pain that then eases, followed by fetal heart rate showing prolonged bradycardia and loss of the previously well-applied presenting part on vaginal exam. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Abruption causes painful bleeding with a tense/tender but intact uterus, not station loss
Chorioamnionitis presents with fever/tachycardia/foul liquor, not acute pain and station loss
Correct — classic uterine rupture triad in a VBAC
Cord prolapse follows membrane rupture with a palpable pulsating cord, not loss of station of the head itself
exp: In a woman attempting VBAC, sudden severe pain that abates, fetal bradycardia, and loss of station of the presenting part on vaginal exam is the classic triad of uterine scar rupture — an obstetric emergency needing immediate laparotomy. Scar tenderness and maternal tachycardia/hypotension may also be present.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman being evaluated for recurrent first-trimester pregnancy loss undergoes MRI pelvis showing a normal, convex external fundal contour with a fibrous septum dividing the endometrial cavity. Which uterine anomaly does this represent?
why: Bicornuate uterus shows an abnormal, indented external fundal contour
Correct
Unicornuate shows a single banana-shaped horn with only half the normal cavity, not a septum
Didelphys shows two completely separate uteri and cervices, not a septum within one cavity
exp: A normal (convex) external fundal contour with an internal septum dividing the cavity defines a septate uterus — the Müllerian anomaly most strongly linked to recurrent miscarriage, corrected by hysteroscopic septal resection.

subject: OBGYN
q: Immediately after a tumultuous vaginal delivery, a woman suddenly develops severe dyspnea, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation, with no preceding fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Pulmonary thromboembolism gives pleuritic chest pain/tachycardia without the immediate florid DIC pattern
Septic shock is preceded by fever/infection signs, absent here
Correct — sudden collapse plus early DIC after tumultuous labor is the classic amniotic fluid embolism picture
Eclampsia presents with seizures and hypertension, not this triad
exp: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare, catastrophic obstetric emergency classically triggered by a tumultuous or instrumented labor, presenting as sudden respiratory distress, cardiovascular collapse, and early disseminated intravascular coagulation (from tissue factor entering maternal circulation) — management is purely supportive (ABC, blood product correction of coagulopathy) since there is no specific antidote.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman on long-term tamoxifen for breast cancer presents with vaginal spotting. Endometrial biopsy shows atypical endometrial hyperplasia. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Continue tamoxifen and repeat biopsy in 6 months
why: Watchful waiting is inappropriate given the high malignancy risk with atypia
Progestogen therapy alone is reserved for hyperplasia without atypia, usually for fertility preservation
LNG-IUS is a fertility-sparing option for hyperplasia without atypia
Correct — hysterectomy is standard once childbearing is complete given the malignancy risk
exp: Tamoxifen has an estrogen-agonist effect on the endometrium, increasing risk of hyperplasia and carcinoma; atypical endometrial hyperplasia carries a substantial risk of concurrent or progression to endometrial cancer, so hysterectomy is standard once childbearing is complete. The concurrent-carcinoma percentage varies by study.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 32-year-old woman has secondary amenorrhea for 8 months with hot flashes and vaginal dryness; FSH is elevated above 40 IU/L on two occasions a month apart. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: PCOS typically shows oligomenorrhea and hyperandrogenism, not an elevated FSH menopausal pattern
Hypothalamic amenorrhea shows LOW gonadotropins, the opposite picture
Correct — elevated FSH with amenorrhea before age 40 defines POI
Asherman syndrome causes amenorrhea with normal hormone levels, a uterine not ovarian problem
exp: Premature ovarian insufficiency is diagnosed by amenorrhea for at least 4 months before age 40 with FSH above 25-40 IU/L on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart, reflecting depleted ovarian follicular reserve; workup should include karyotype (e.g., Turner mosaicism, Fragile X premutation) and autoimmune screening.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and foul-smelling lochia 10 days after an otherwise uncomplicated vaginal delivery, with a subinvoluted, tender uterus and low-grade fever. What is the most likely cause of this secondary postpartum hemorrhage?
opts: Retained products of conception with endometritis
why: Uterine atony is the classic cause of primary (within 24h) PPH, not a day-10 presentation
Correct — retained products/endometritis is the commonest cause of secondary PPH
A genital tract laceration bleeds immediately postpartum, not after a 10-day delay
Amniotic fluid embolism is an acute peripartum collapse syndrome, not a delayed bleeding presentation
exp: Secondary (delayed) PPH occurs between 24 hours and 6 weeks postpartum and is most commonly due to retained products of conception and/or endometritis, presenting with subinvolution, foul lochia, and fever; management is antibiotics plus ultrasound-guided evacuation of retained products — a distinct entity from primary PPH's atony/trauma/coagulopathy causes.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 32 weeks gestation complains of severe generalized pruritus, worse on palms and soles, with no rash, and mildly deranged liver enzymes. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Check serum bile acids and start ursodeoxycholic acid
Start antihistamines only, no further workup
why: Pruritus of this pattern with deranged LFTs needs workup, not reassurance alone
Immediate cesarean is not indicated on this presentation alone
Correct - intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy diagnosis and first-line treatment
Antihistamines don't address the underlying cholestasis or fetal risk
exp: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy classically causes pruritus of palms/soles without a primary rash in the third trimester; diagnosis is confirmed by elevated fasting serum bile acids, treatment is ursodeoxycholic acid, and delivery is typically planned by 37-38 weeks given the stillbirth risk with rising bile acid levels.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 46-year-old woman presents with heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding for 3 months, with no prior gynecological complaints. What is the most appropriate first-line investigation given her age?
opts: Reassurance and observation for 6 more months
why: Correct - the standard first-line workup for AUB in a woman over 45
CA-125 is a nonspecific ovarian tumour marker, not first-line for AUB workup
Diagnostic laparoscopy is invasive and not first-line here
Observation risks missing endometrial pathology given her age
exp: In abnormal uterine bleeding, age is a key trigger for endometrial evaluation - women over 45 (or younger with risk factors like obesity, PCOS, or tamoxifen use) should have transvaginal ultrasound plus endometrial sampling to exclude hyperplasia or carcinoma before starting purely symptomatic hormonal management.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman is found on transvaginal USG to have a complex multilocular ovarian cyst with solid areas and free fluid (ultrasound score 3), and her serum CA-125 is 250 U/mL. Using the Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI = U x M x CA-125, with M = 3 for postmenopausal status), what is her calculated RMI and the appropriate next step?
opts: RMI 750 — moderate risk, repeat USG in 6 weeks
RMI cannot be calculated without knowing tumour size
RMI 2250 — high risk, refer to gynaecologic oncology
why: Miscalculates the product; 250 alone is not U times M times CA-125 here
Underestimates the product of 3 times 3 times 250
Tumour size is not an input in RMI I/II/III, the version used here; only RMI 4 adds it
Correct — 3 (U) x 3 (M) x 250 (CA-125) = 2250, a high-risk score
exp: RMI = U x M x CA-125, with U=3 when two or more of five ultrasound features are present. An RMI above 200 is high risk and mandates referral to a gynaecologic oncology multidisciplinary team for staging rather than routine follow-up.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 24-year-old at 10 weeks by dates presents with hyperemesis and vaginal bleeding; her uterus is larger than dates, serum beta-hCG is markedly elevated, and USG shows a diffuse snowstorm pattern with no fetal parts, along with bilateral enlarged cystic ovaries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Complete hydatidiform mole with theca lutein cysts
why: Threatened abortion does not explain the markedly raised hCG, snowstorm pattern, or theca lutein cysts
A demised twin pregnancy would still show fetal parts on USG, unlike a complete mole
Correct — classic complete molar pregnancy presentation
Ectopic pregnancy shows an empty uterus with an adnexal mass, not an enlarged uterus with a snowstorm pattern
exp: Complete hydatidiform mole arises from fertilisation of an empty ovum, producing diffuse trophoblastic proliferation with no fetal tissue, markedly elevated beta-hCG, a uterus larger than dates, and the classic snowstorm sonographic appearance; the very high hCG drives bilateral theca lutein cysts that usually regress after evacuation.

subject: OBGYN
q: A primigravida at 32 weeks has blood pressure of 150/100 mmHg on two occasions 4 hours apart, with normal urine protein on dipstick, but new-onset thrombocytopenia (platelets 90,000/microL) and liver transaminases 3x the upper limit of normal. According to current ACOG diagnostic criteria, this presentation:
opts: Does not qualify as preeclampsia without proteinuria
Requires a 24-hour urine collection before any diagnosis can be made
Qualifies as preeclampsia, but cannot be labelled with severe features unless BP reaches 160/110 mmHg
Qualifies as preeclampsia, since end-organ dysfunction can substitute for proteinuria
why: This reflects older criteria; current ACOG guidance allows diagnosis without proteinuria if end-organ dysfunction is present
A 24-hour urine collection is unnecessary once end-organ dysfunction criteria are already met
Thrombocytopenia <100,000/microL and transaminases 2x normal or more are themselves severe features, irrespective of BP range
Correct — end-organ dysfunction is an accepted alternative diagnostic pathway
exp: Current ACOG criteria no longer require proteinuria for preeclampsia diagnosis when new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks is accompanied by maternal end-organ dysfunction — thrombocytopenia (<100,000/microL), transaminases >=2x ULN, renal insufficiency, pulmonary oedema, or new cerebral/visual symptoms. This patient's findings are themselves severe features, so she has preeclampsia with severe features regardless of BP range.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 37 weeks gestation has a singleton frank breech presentation, adequate liquor volume, no previous uterine scar, and a reactive non-stress test. Before offering either a trial of vaginal breech delivery or an elective caesarean section, the recommended intervention to attempt first is:
opts: Induction of labour in the breech position
why: Immediate caesarean bypasses first attempting version, which can avoid an operative delivery altogether
Internal podalic version is an intrapartum manoeuvre mainly for a second twin, not external repositioning before labour
Correct — ECV is recommended first-line for an eligible breech pregnancy at term
Deliberately inducing labour in breech position without first attempting version increases vaginal breech delivery risks
exp: External cephalic version, performed at or after 36-37 weeks under tocolysis with emergency caesarean facilities available, manually turns the fetus from breech to cephalic through the maternal abdominal wall; when successful, it substantially reduces the need for caesarean delivery.

subject: OBGYN
q: A Rh-negative primigravida with an Rh-positive partner has an uneventful antenatal course. At what time point(s) should anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis be administered to prevent alloimmunization, assuming no sensitizing event occurs?
opts: Only within 72 hours after delivery of an Rh-positive baby
Only if the antibody screen is already positive
At 28 weeks gestation and again within 72 hours postpartum if the baby is Rh-positive
why: Postpartum-only dosing was the older single-dose protocol
Anti-D is prophylactic, not given once antibodies already indicate sensitization has occurred
12 weeks is too early and not the standard antenatal dosing point
Correct, routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 weeks plus postpartum dose if baby is Rh-positive
exp: Routine antenatal anti-D at 28 weeks, in addition to postpartum dosing, further reduces the residual 1-2 percent sensitization risk left by postpartum-only prophylaxis, and additional doses are given after any sensitizing event (APH, ECV, amniocentesis, abdominal trauma) regardless of gestation. The exact dose varies by product.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman complains of chronic vulvar itching for several months. Examination shows thin, white, atrophic parchment-paper plaques in a figure-of-eight distribution around the vulva and perianal skin, with loss of normal labial architecture. Biopsy is planned before starting topical corticosteroid therapy, primarily to exclude which complication?
why: Correct, lichen sclerosus has an established malignant potential for SCC, mandating biopsy of atypical areas before treatment
Melanoma is a rarer vulvar malignancy with a different pigmented appearance, not linked to this parchment-white figure-of-eight picture
Bartholin gland carcinoma presents as a discrete gland mass, not diffuse atrophic plaques
Paget disease of the vulva presents as an eczematous, weepy erythematous plaque, not parchment-white atrophy
exp: Lichen sclerosus carries a lifetime risk of roughly 4-5 percent for progression to vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, so biopsy of any thickened, ulcerated, or non-responding area is standard before or at the start of potent topical corticosteroid (e.g., clobetasol propionate) therapy to exclude coexisting malignancy or VIN.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 29 weeks gestation presents in preterm labor with regular contractions and cervical dilation of 3 cm. Fetal heart rate is reassuring. Along with tocolysis, which intervention most improves neonatal outcome if delivery occurs within the next week?
opts: Prophylactic antibiotics to the mother regardless of membrane status
High-dose oral iron and calcium supplementation
Immediate cesarean delivery to avoid labor-related fetal stress
A single course of antenatal corticosteroids (e.g., betamethasone)
why: Prophylactic antibiotics are indicated for PPROM or confirmed infection, not this scenario with intact membranes
Iron/calcium supplementation has no role in accelerating fetal lung maturity
Preterm labor alone with reassuring fetal status is not an indication for cesarean
Correct, antenatal corticosteroids reduce RDS, IVH, and neonatal mortality
exp: Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 12 mg IM x2 doses 24h apart, or dexamethasone 6 mg IM x4 doses 12h apart) given between 24+0 and 34+0 weeks to women at risk of preterm delivery within 7 days is one of the most effective, cheap, evidence-based interventions in obstetrics, dramatically reducing RDS and neonatal mortality.

subject: OBGYN
q: On partograph monitoring of a primigravida in active labor, the cervimetric (dilation) curve crosses to the right of the action line (4 hours to the right of the alert line). What is the appropriate next step?
opts: Continue routine observation, as this is expected in normal labor
Wait for the curve to cross the alert line again before taking any action
Discharge and reassess in the outpatient clinic after 24 hours
Reassess for cephalopelvic disproportion/obstructed labor and consider intervention (e.g., augmentation or cesarean)
why: Crossing the action line signals a significant delay requiring active evaluation, not routine reassurance
The action line is crossed after already crossing the alert line 4 hours earlier, so waiting further risks compromise
Labor is an acute intrapartum event; outpatient deferral is inappropriate and unsafe
Correct, reassess the 3 Ps (power, passage, passenger) and decide on augmentation or cesarean
exp: The WHO partograph's alert line (drawn from 4 cm dilation, 1 cm/hour) prompts transfer to a facility with obstetric/surgical capability if crossed, while the action line (drawn 4 hours to the right) is the threshold at which active intervention decisions must be made - a core tool for detecting prolonged/obstructed labor early.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 34-year-old woman with menorrhagia undergoes hysteroscopy, which shows a submucosal fibroid entirely within the endometrial cavity with no myometrial extension. What is its FIGO leiomyoma classification?
why: Correct — entirely intracavitary with no myometrial component is Type 0.
Wrong — Type 1 has some (<50%) intramural extension.
Wrong — Type 2 has ≥50% intramural extension.
Wrong — Type 3 touches the endometrium but is entirely intramural, not intracavitary.
exp: The FIGO leiomyoma classification grades submucosal fibroids by myometrial extension: Type 0 is pedunculated submucosal, entirely intracavitary; Type 1 is <50% intramural; Type 2 is ≥50% intramural; Type 3 contacts the endometrium but is entirely intramural. Type 0/1 fibroids are the most amenable to hysteroscopic resection and have the greatest impact on menorrhagia/fertility.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman has heavy vaginal bleeding immediately after delivery of the placenta, with a soft, boggy, poorly contracted uterus on palpation. Which of the 4 T's of postpartum hemorrhage is the most likely cause?
why: Wrong — retained tissue typically presents with an incompletely delivered or irregular placenta, or ongoing bleeding despite a contracted uterus.
Wrong — trauma/laceration causes bleeding with a well-contracted (firm) uterus, not a boggy one.
Wrong — thrombin/coagulopathy causes continued oozing and failure to clot, not specifically uterine sponginess.
Correct — a soft/boggy, poorly contracted uterus with bleeding is uterine atony, the commonest PPH cause.
exp: The 4 T's of postpartum hemorrhage are Tone (uterine atony — the most common cause, roughly 70% of cases), Tissue (retained placenta/clots), Trauma (cervical/vaginal/perineal lacerations, uterine rupture), and Thrombin (coagulopathy). A soft, boggy, atonic uterus on exam is the hallmark of tone-related PPH, managed with uterine massage, oxytocin, and second-line uterotonics (carboprost, misoprostol).

subject: OBGYN
q: A 45-year-old with biopsy-proven cervical carcinoma has a tumour confined to the cervix with no parametrial extension, clinically measuring 4.5 cm. What is the FIGO stage?
why: Wrong — IIA requires extension into the upper vagina, which is absent here (the tumour is confined to the cervix).
Correct — confined to the cervix, 4 cm or larger, is IB3 per FIGO 2018.
Wrong — IIB requires parametrial invasion, explicitly absent in this stem.
Wrong — IA2 is a microscopic lesion (stromal invasion 3-5 mm), inconsistent with a palpable 4.5 cm mass.
exp: FIGO 2018 cervical cancer staging: Stage I is disease confined to the cervix, with IB subdivided by tumour size (IB1 under 2cm, IB2 2-4cm, IB3 4cm or larger). Stage II extends beyond the uterus (IIA upper two-thirds vaginal extension without parametrial invasion; IIB parametrial invasion). A 4.5cm tumour confined to the cervix, without vaginal or parametrial extension, is IB3.

subject: OBGYN
q: A primigravida at 41 weeks with a reactive NST is planned for induction of labour. On vaginal examination, the cervix is 1 cm dilated, 30% effaced, firm in consistency, posterior in position, and the head is at station -3. What is the most appropriate next step in her management?
opts: Favorable Bishop score (8 or more) — proceed directly with amniotomy and oxytocin infusion
Score 6 to 7 — a Foley catheter balloon alone is adequate, no pharmacological agent is needed
Bishop scoring is not used to guide the induction method in primigravidae
Unfavorable Bishop score (5 or less) — perform cervical ripening with PGE2 gel or misoprostol before oxytocin
why: A favorable score of 8 or more does not apply here — her computed score is near 0.
Her score is far below 6 to 7, and pharmacological ripening rather than Foley alone is standard at this severity.
Bishop scoring guides induction method in all women, including primigravidae.
Correct — an unfavorable score mandates cervical ripening before oxytocin.
exp: The Bishop score grades cervical favorability using dilation, effacement, consistency, position, and station. This patient scores roughly 1, clearly unfavorable (5 or less), which predicts higher failed-induction and caesarean risk unless the cervix is first ripened with PGE2 or misoprostol before oxytocin is started. A score of 8 or more approximates spontaneous-labour success and allows oxytocin with or without amniotomy directly.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 24-year-old sexually active woman with a recent history of treated pelvic inflammatory disease presents with sharp, pleuritic right upper quadrant pain and mild right hypochondrial tenderness. Liver function tests and ultrasound of the gallbladder are normal. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
why: correct — RUQ pain with a recent PID history and normal LFTs/gallbladder is the classic perihepatitis picture
Cholecystitis would show gallbladder wall thickening/stones on ultrasound, which is absent here
Budd-Chiari presents with hepatomegaly, ascites, and deranged LFTs from venous outflow obstruction
Pneumonia would show respiratory signs and a chest X-ray abnormality, not linked to a PID history
exp: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatitis caused by direct spread of Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae from the pelvis along the paracolic gutter to the liver capsule, producing violin-string adhesions between the liver and abdominal wall/diaphragm. It presents with RUQ pain mimicking cholecystitis but with normal liver enzymes and a normal gallbladder — the PID history is the clue.

subject: OBGYN
q: A multigravida with a footling breech presentation has spontaneous rupture of membranes. Immediately afterward the fetal heart rate drops to 80/min, and vaginal examination reveals a pulsatile cord below the presenting part. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Apply fundal pressure to expedite vaginal delivery
Perform artificial rupture of membranes of the second sac if this is a twin gestation
Elevate the presenting part manually and position the patient in knee-chest/Trendelenburg position while arranging emergency cesarean
why: Oxytocin augmentation worsens compression by increasing contractions, contraindicated here
Fundal pressure would push the presenting part further onto the cord, worsening compression
Rupturing the second sac is irrelevant and does not address the presenting cord compression
correct — relieving compression plus expedited cesarean is the standard emergency response
exp: This is umbilical cord prolapse, an obstetric emergency where cord compression between the presenting part and the pelvis causes acute fetal hypoxia — breech and other malpresentations are major risk factors, especially after membrane rupture. Immediate management is to relieve compression by manually elevating the presenting part off the cord and positioning the mother knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg, while arranging emergency cesarean delivery.

subject: OBGYN
q: During a vaginal examination in active labour, the umbilical cord is felt pulsating below the presenting part with the membranes ruptured. What is the immediate first step?
opts: Start oxytocin augmentation to expedite vaginal delivery
Perform artificial rupture of membranes to confirm the diagnosis
Manually elevate the presenting part off the cord while arranging emergency caesarean
Apply firm fundal pressure to push the presenting part down
why: Wrong — oxytocin augmentation increases contractions and worsens cord compression.
Wrong — membranes are already ruptured, ARM is irrelevant and wastes time.
Correct — elevate the presenting part off the cord and rush for emergency caesarean.
Wrong — fundal pressure would push the presenting part further onto the cord, worsening compression.
exp: Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency: keep the examining hand in the vagina elevating the presenting part off the cord (knee-chest or Trendelenburg position) to relieve compression while arranging immediate caesarean delivery, since fetal hypoxia from cord compression/vasospasm progresses within minutes.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 28-year-old woman develops abdominal distension, bilateral ovarian enlargement, and breathlessness five days after a gonadotropin-triggered ovulation induction cycle for IVF. Her hematocrit is elevated and ultrasound shows ascites. What is the diagnosis?
why: Torsion typically presents with acute unilateral pain and a whirlpool sign on Doppler, not bilateral enlargement with ascites and hemoconcentration.
Correct — OHSS follows gonadotropin stimulation; VEGF-mediated capillary hyperpermeability causes ascites/pleural effusion, hemoconcentration, and bilateral cystic ovarian enlargement.
A ruptured ectopic presents with hemoperitoneum, hypotension, and a positive pregnancy test, not this fluid-shift picture after ovulation induction.
Meigs syndrome is ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion, unrelated to gonadotropin stimulation and typically seen in older women.
exp: OHSS is an iatrogenic complication of gonadotropin-triggered ovulation induction/IVF, driven by VEGF-mediated increased capillary permeability — leading to third-spacing (ascites, pleural effusion), hemoconcentration (a key severity marker on hematocrit), and bilateral ovarian enlargement. Severe OHSS carries a thromboembolism risk and is managed with careful fluid/albumin replacement, not aggressive diuresis.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 58-year-old woman presents with postmenopausal bleeding. Ultrasound shows a solid-cystic right ovarian mass, and endometrial biopsy shows endometrial hyperplasia. Serum inhibin B is markedly elevated, and histopathology of the ovarian mass shows Call-Exner bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Krukenberg tumour is a bilateral signet-ring-cell metastasis, usually from a gastric primary, not a hormonally active tumour with Call-Exner bodies
Dysgerminoma is a germ-cell tumour of young women marked by LDH, not an oestrogen-producing stromal tumour
Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid) is a benign germ-cell tumour with a Rokitansky nodule, not hormonally active
Correct — the oestrogenic effect on the endometrium plus Call-Exner bodies and inhibin B are diagnostic
exp: Granulosa cell tumour is an oestrogen-secreting sex-cord stromal tumour of the ovary; the excess oestrogen drives endometrial hyperplasia (or carcinoma) and postmenopausal bleeding. Call-Exner bodies on histology and elevated inhibin B (also used clinically to monitor recurrence) are the classic diagnostic pairing.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 17-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. She has normal breast development and normal axillary/pubic hair. Pelvic exam reveals a blind-ending short vagina; ultrasound shows an absent uterus with normal-appearing ovaries. Karyotype is 46,XX. Which condition best explains this presentation?
why: AIS has a 46,XY karyotype with intra-abdominal/inguinal testes and sparse axillary/pubic hair from androgen-receptor defect - doesn't fit a 46,XX girl with normal hair
Turner syndrome (45,X) presents with streak gonads and absent secondary sexual development, unlike this normally developed girl
Correct - Mullerian agenesis with normal ovarian origin explains normal secondary sexual characters, normal karyotype, and absent uterus
Imperforate hymen presents with cyclical pain from hematocolpos and a bulging bluish membrane, with a normal uterus present on ultrasound - not an absent uterus
exp: MRKH syndrome is congenital agenesis of the Mullerian ducts, causing an absent/rudimentary uterus and upper vagina with normal ovarian function - since the ovaries develop from the genital ridge, not the Mullerian ducts, secondary sexual characters and karyotype remain normal. Pubic/axillary hair being present is the key bedside discriminator from androgen insensitivity syndrome.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 28-year-old woman at 20 weeks gestation with a known 8 cm intramural fibroid presents with acute severe localized abdominal pain, low-grade fever, and tenderness directly over the fibroid. Ultrasound shows no fetal compromise. What is the most likely cause?
why: Torsion occurs with pedunculated subserosal fibroids (not the intramural type here) and produces more diffuse peritoneal signs
Chorioamnionitis causes diffuse uterine tenderness with fever, typically alongside membrane rupture, not tenderness localized to a discrete mass
Abruption presents with vaginal bleeding and a diffusely tense, tender uterus with fetal compromise, not focal mass tenderness
Correct - hemorrhagic infarction of the fibroid as the growing pregnant uterus outstrips its blood supply, managed conservatively
exp: Red degeneration is hemorrhagic infarction of a fibroid, classically occurring in the second/third trimester as the rapidly enlarging pregnant uterus outstrips the fibroid's blood supply; it presents with acute focal pain and low-grade fever localized to the mass and is managed conservatively with analgesia and rest, not surgery, as it is self-limiting.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 24-year-old sexually active woman presents with 4 days of lower abdominal pain, fever, and vaginal discharge. Examination shows bilateral adnexal tenderness, cervical motion tenderness, and a tender right adnexal mass on bimanual exam. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure and repeat pelvic exam in 1 week
Start oral doxycycline alone and review in 2 weeks
Transvaginal ultrasound to look for a tubo-ovarian abscess, then admit for IV antibiotics
why: Untreated PID/TOA risks rupture and sepsis and cannot simply be observed
Oral therapy alone is inadequate once a tubo-ovarian abscess is suspected — IV therapy and imaging are needed
Correct — image first to confirm TOA, then IV antibiotics is the standard first-line sequence
Surgery is reserved for rupture or failed medical therapy, not first-line
exp: A tender adnexal mass in a patient with clinical PID raises suspicion for a tubo-ovarian abscess. Confirm on transvaginal ultrasound, then admit for IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic cover; surgery/drainage is reserved for rupture or non-response.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 34 weeks gestation, with a known velamentous cord insertion on a prior ultrasound, has sudden painless vaginal bleeding immediately after spontaneous rupture of membranes. The cardiotocograph shows a sudden fetal bradycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Vasa previa with fetal vessel rupture
why: Abruption typically causes painful bleeding with a tense, tender uterus, not painless bleeding timed exactly to membrane rupture
Correct — painless bleeding at ROM plus sudden fetal bradycardia in a known velamentous cord insertion is the classic vasa previa picture
Placenta previa causes painless bleeding but is not typically triggered at the instant of membrane rupture, nor does it cause abrupt fetal deterioration from fetal blood loss
Uterine rupture usually occurs in a scarred uterus with severe pain and loss of contractions, not simply at ROM
exp: Vasa previa (fetal vessels crossing the internal os unprotected, often from a velamentous cord insertion) classically presents with painless bleeding at the moment of membrane rupture plus acute fetal compromise, because the bleeding is fetal blood — an obstetric emergency needing immediate caesarean delivery.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 48-year-old woman presents with bilateral solid, mobile ovarian masses on ultrasound; histopathology reveals mucin-secreting signet-ring cells within a cellular stroma. Which primary site is most likely?
why: Primary ovarian mucinous tumours are usually unilateral, cystic masses — not bilateral solid signet-ring metastases
Brenner tumour shows transitional-cell-like nests (Walthard cell rests), not signet-ring cells
Correct — classic Krukenberg picture, commonest primary is gastric
Cervical carcinoma rarely produces this bilateral signet-ring metastatic pattern
exp: Krukenberg tumour = bilateral, solid, mobile ovarian metastases containing mucin-filled signet-ring cells; the stomach is the commonest primary (about 70 percent), followed by colon and breast. Bilaterality plus signet-ring histology should always trigger a search for a GI primary rather than treatment as a primary ovarian cancer.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 24-year-old woman presents with mild lower abdominal pain. Pelvic ultrasound shows a right ovarian mass with a hyperechoic nodule projecting into the cyst lumen, showing acoustic shadowing, along with a fat-fluid level. This is most typical of:
why: Correct - Rokitansky protuberance with acoustic shadowing (tooth/hair) and a fat-fluid level are pathognomonic dermoid cyst findings.
Endometrioma shows homogeneous low-level internal ground-glass echoes from old blood, without a calcified or shadowing nodule.
Serous cystadenoma is a thin-walled, unilocular, purely anechoic cyst with no internal nodule.
Mucinous cystadenoma is typically multilocular with fine, low-level stained-glass internal echoes, not a shadowing dermoid plug.
exp: A shadowing dermoid plug (Rokitansky nodule) plus a fat-fluid level on ultrasound is the classic sonographic signature of a mature cystic teratoma - the commonest benign ovarian germ cell tumour in young women, and one prone to torsion because of its heterogeneous, mobile content.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 38-year-old woman from a rural area undergoes opportunistic cervical cancer screening at a PHC where cytology facilities are unavailable. Which low-cost screening test is recommended?
why: Pap smear requires a cytology lab and trained cytopathologist, unavailable at this PHC per the stem
Colposcopy is a secondary diagnostic tool to localise lesions after a positive screen, needing a specialist and equipment
Correct - VIA needs only acetic acid and a torch, suited to low-resource settings
HPV DNA testing is more sensitive but costly and lab-dependent, used in better-resourced settings
exp: VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid) is India's recommended low-cost, same-day, infrastructure-independent cervical cancer screening test for PHC-level settings, performed by trained nurses/health workers, allowing screen-and-treat with cryotherapy in the same visit if positive.

subject: OBGYN
q: During vaginal delivery of a macrosomic infant, the fetal head retracts against the perineum immediately after delivery (turtle sign) and gentle traction fails to deliver the anterior shoulder, consistent with shoulder dystocia. What is the most appropriate first maneuver to attempt?
why: Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia as it worsens impaction and risks uterine rupture.
Correct - McRoberts maneuver (hyperflexion and abduction of maternal hips) with suprapubic pressure is first-line and resolves most cases.
Zavanelli maneuver (cephalic replacement for emergency cesarean) is a last resort, not a first step.
Cesarean section is not feasible once the fetal head has already delivered; management must proceed vaginally.
exp: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency; the first maneuver is McRoberts positioning combined with suprapubic pressure, which resolves the majority of cases by straightening the sacrum and rotating the pubic symphysis to free the anterior shoulder. Fundal pressure is contraindicated. Escalate through internal rotation maneuvers (Rubin, Woods screw) and delivery of the posterior arm before considering last-resort options.

subject: OBGYN
q: A pregnant woman at 24 weeks gestation undergoes a single-step 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (DIPSI method, non-fasting) as recommended under India's national guidelines. What 2-hour plasma glucose value confirms gestational diabetes mellitus?
why: 100 mg/dL is closer to a fasting glucose threshold, not the DIPSI 2-hour cutoff.
Correct - the DIPSI single-step 75 g OGTT uses a 2-hour plasma glucose of 140 mg/dL or more as the diagnostic cutoff for GDM.
180 mg/dL is closer to a 1-hour glucose challenge threshold used in other two-step protocols, not the DIPSI 2-hour value.
200 mg/dL is the general diabetes diagnostic threshold, too high for the DIPSI GDM cutoff.
exp: Under India's national DIPSI (Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Group India) protocol, gestational diabetes is diagnosed with a single-step, non-fasting 75 g oral glucose load followed by a 2-hour plasma glucose measurement; a value of 140 mg/dL or more is diagnostic. This single-step approach was adopted nationally because it avoids the logistics of fasting testing in resource-limited antenatal settings.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 42-year-old multiparous woman presents with progressively worsening dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia for 2 years. Examination reveals a diffusely enlarged, globular, tender uterus with no discrete masses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Leiomyoma typically gives an irregular, non-tender uterus with discrete masses, not diffuse globular enlargement
Endometrial polyp does not cause diffuse uterine enlargement
Correct — a diffusely enlarged, globular, tender uterus in a parous woman with dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia is classic adenomyosis
Chronic PID tenderness is usually accompanied by adnexal involvement or an infection history, not a diffusely globular uterus
exp: Adenomyosis classically presents in a parous woman over 40 with a diffusely enlarged, globular, boggy, tender uterus plus dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia — contrast with leiomyoma, which gives an irregular, non-tender uterus with discrete masses. MRI shows a widened junctional zone (over 12 mm); definitive diagnosis is on hysterectomy specimen histology.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 13-year-old girl presents with cyclical lower abdominal pain for six months but has never menstruated. She has normal breast development and pubic hair, and a bluish bulging membrane is visible at the introitus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: MRKH causes primary amenorrhoea without cyclical pain, since the uterus is absent or rudimentary with no menstrual blood to trap, and no bulging membrane is seen.
Androgen insensitivity syndrome shows absent or sparse pubic/axillary hair and no uterus or menstrual potential at all.
Correct - normal secondary sexual characters with cyclical pain from hematocolpos and a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus is imperforate hymen.
A transverse vaginal septum also causes hematocolpos but sits higher in the vaginal canal, so the hymen itself appears normal on inspection rather than bulging at the introitus.
exp: Cyclical abdominal pain with primary amenorrhoea, normal secondary sexual characters, and a visible bluish bulging membrane at the introitus points to imperforate hymen causing hematocolpos (trapped menstrual blood). It is a simple obstructive anomaly cured by cruciate hymenotomy - always examine the external genitalia before ordering imaging in a girl with cyclical pain and no periods.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a painful, fluctuant swelling at the posterior aspect of the left labium majus, most marked at the 4-5 o'clock position, causing difficulty sitting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — classic location and presentation
Sebaceous cysts are usually non-tender unless secondarily infected and are not confined to this specific location
Inguinal hernia presents as a reducible swelling that changes with straining, not typically painful and fluctuant
Gartner's duct cyst arises from mesonephric duct remnants along the anterolateral vaginal wall, usually asymptomatic and not at the posterior introitus
exp: Bartholin's gland abscess classically presents as a unilateral, tender, fluctuant swelling at the posterior introitus at the 4-5 or 7-8 o'clock position, matching the location of the paired Bartholin's glands. Management is incision and drainage with marsupialization or Word catheter placement, not antibiotics alone, to reduce recurrence.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 32-year-old G3P2 at 34 weeks with pregnancy-induced hypertension presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding. The uterus is tense, tender and hypertonic, and the CTG shows late decelerations. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Placenta previa causes painless bright-red bleeding with a soft uterus, not this tense/tender picture.
Vasa previa presents with painless bleeding at membrane rupture and fetal bradycardia, not maternal tetany or pain.
Correct — pain, hypertonic tender uterus, hypertension risk factor and fetal distress together indicate abruption.
Uterine rupture typically occurs intrapartum in a scarred uterus with loss of contractions and station, not this antepartum picture.
exp: Abruptio placentae classically presents with painful bleeding plus a tense, tender, hypertonic uterus and fetal distress, often precipitated by hypertensive disorders of pregnancy — the key bedside discriminator from placenta previa's painless bleeding and soft uterus.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 28-year-old woman develops secondary amenorrhoea and cyclical pelvic pain three months after a vigorous postpartum curettage performed for retained products of conception. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Premature ovarian insufficiency causes amenorrhoea with low oestrogen and vasomotor symptoms, unrelated to a recent curettage

Correct — vigorous endometrial curettage, especially postpartum, damages the basal layer and causes intrauterine synechiae, producing amenorrhoea or hypomenorrhoea with cyclical pain from trapped blood
PCOS causes oligo or amenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovaries, with no link to a curettage history
Endometriosis causes cyclical pain and dysmenorrhoea but not secondary amenorrhoea, and has no direct link to curettage
exp: Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions) should be suspected in secondary amenorrhoea or cyclical pain following aggressive uterine instrumentation, especially postpartum curettage; diagnose with hysteroscopy (gold standard) or HSG/saline sonohysterography, and treat with hysteroscopic adhesiolysis.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 42-year-old woman has heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding for 8 months. Pelvic ultrasound shows a well-defined intramural mass distorting the endometrial cavity, with normal coagulation studies. Under the FIGO PALM-COEIN classification of abnormal uterine bleeding, this cause is categorised as which subtype?
exp: FIGO's PALM-COEIN system splits AUB causes into structural (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia) and non-structural (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not-yet-classified) groups. A discrete, well-defined intramural mass distorting the cavity - as opposed to the diffusely thickened, poorly marginated myometrium of adenomyosis - is classified as leiomyoma (L).

subject: OBGYN
q: A 28-year-old nulliparous woman presents with progressively worsening cyclical dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, and 2 years of infertility. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a unilateral ovarian cyst with homogeneous, low-level ground-glass internal echoes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Wrong — a tubo-ovarian abscess gives fever, acute pain and a complex multiloculated mass
Wrong — a dermoid shows heterogeneous echoes with a Rokitansky nodule and shadowing, not homogeneous ground glass
Wrong — a corpus luteal cyst resolves in weeks and does not explain 2 years of infertility
Correct — cyclical pain, deep dyspareunia and infertility with a ground-glass (chocolate) cyst is an endometrioma
exp: The triad of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility with a ground-glass (chocolate cyst) appearance on TVS is classic for an endometrioma. CA-125 is often raised but is not diagnostic; laparoscopy remains the gold standard for confirming endometriosis.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with sudden painless bright-red vaginal bleeding and a soft, non-tender uterus; fetal heart rate is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate next step?
opts: Placenta previa - avoid digital vaginal exam, confirm with ultrasound
Abruptio placentae - proceed to immediate delivery
why: Correct — painless bright-red bleeding with a soft uterus is placenta previa; avoid a digital exam and confirm by ultrasound
Wrong — abruption gives painful bleeding with a tender, hypertonic uterus and often fetal distress
Wrong — vasa previa bleeds at membrane rupture with fetal distress and needs emergency caesarean, not amnioinfusion
Wrong — uterine rupture gives severe pain, loss of contour and fetal distress
exp: Painless bright-red bleeding with a soft, non-tender uterus in the third trimester is classic for placenta previa. Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated until previa is excluded by ultrasound, since it can provoke catastrophic hemorrhage from the low-lying placenta.

subject: OBGYN
q: A primigravida at 38 weeks by reliable first-trimester dating has a growth scan showing BPD and HC corresponding to roughly 32-33 weeks, while AC corresponds to 37 weeks and FL to 38 weeks. What does this biometric pattern most likely indicate?
opts: Symmetric fetal growth restriction affecting all parameters equally
Isolated fetal microcephaly with otherwise normal somatic growth - the reverse of the head-sparing pattern
A technical ultrasound calibration error, with no true pathology implied
why: Wrong: in asymmetric FGR the AC lags and the head is spared, the opposite of this pattern.
Wrong: symmetric FGR reduces all parameters, but AC and FL are on dates here.
Correct: head lagging 5–6 weeks while AC and FL track dates is the signature of isolated microcephaly.
Wrong: a consistent multi-parameter pattern is not explained by calibration error.
exp: Head lagging while abdomen and femur track dates is the reverse of placental-insufficiency FGR. In head-sparing (asymmetric) FGR the AC drops first and the head is protected; here the head is the affected parameter, which is the biometric signature of isolated microcephaly. Do not force every biometric mismatch into the IUGR framework.

subject: OBGYN
q: In placental-insufficiency-driven asymmetric fetal growth restriction, which biometric parameter becomes abnormal earliest and most severely?
why: Wrong: HC is spared by brain-sparing redistribution until late.
Correct: AC (liver glycogen and subcutaneous fat) is affected first and most severely.
Wrong: femur length is usually preserved until late or severe disease.
Wrong: BPD, like HC, is protected by brain sparing.
exp: Abdominal circumference is the first and most severely affected parameter in asymmetric FGR, because it reflects fetal liver glycogen and subcutaneous fat, both of which are sacrificed early. Brain-sparing redistribution protects head growth until late or severe disease, so a normal HC never rules out FGR.

subject: OBGYN
q: Which Doppler finding is expected in true head-sparing (asymmetric) FGR from placental insufficiency, and would NOT be expected in a fetus whose head alone is lagging with normal AC and FL?
opts: Raised umbilical artery resistance with reduced or absent end-diastolic flow, and a reduced cerebroplacental ratio
Normal umbilical artery and MCA Doppler throughout
Reduced resistance in both uterine arteries
why: Correct: raised umbilical artery resistance with a falling cerebroplacental ratio is the Doppler signature of placental insufficiency.
Wrong: normal Doppler argues against placental insufficiency and fits a primary head-growth problem.
Wrong: placental-insufficiency FGR causes oligohydramnios, not a raised AFI.
Wrong: low uterine artery resistance is the normal pregnancy finding; placental insufficiency raises it.
exp: Raised umbilical artery resistance with a falling cerebroplacental ratio (MCA PI divided by UA PI) is the Doppler signature of placental insufficiency. A purely head-growth process does not alter these vessels, so normal Doppler in a small-headed fetus argues against FGR and points towards microcephaly.

subject: OBGYN
q: What is the generally accepted ultrasound threshold for labelling a fetus microcephalic?
opts: Head circumference below the 50th percentile for gestational age
Head circumference 2 SD below the mean on a single measurement
Head circumference 3 SD or more below the mean (or below the 3rd percentile) for gestational age on a validated chart
Biparietal diameter alone below the 10th percentile
why: Wrong: below the 50th percentile would flag half of all normal fetuses.
Wrong: 2 SD is the looser postnatal cutoff and over-calls normal fetuses antenatally.
Correct: antenatal microcephaly is HC 3 SD or more below the mean (or below the 3rd percentile), confirmed on repeat scan.
Wrong: BPD alone is distorted by head shape (dolichocephaly); HC is the parameter to use.
exp: Fetal microcephaly is defined as HC at least 3 SD below the mean for gestational age on a validated chart; the 2 SD cutoff used postnatally is too loose antenatally and over-calls normal fetuses. Confirm on a repeat scan about 2 weeks later, and never label on BPD alone, which is distorted by head shape (dolichocephaly).

subject: OBGYN
q: Which congenital infection is the single most common infective cause of fetal and neonatal microcephaly worldwide?
why: Wrong: toxoplasmosis is a TORCH cause but far less common than CMV worldwide.
Wrong: rubella causes microcephaly but has fallen sharply with vaccination.
Correct: congenital CMV is the commonest infective cause of microcephaly and of non-genetic SNHL.
Wrong: HSV causes severe neonatal disease but rarely microcephaly.
exp: Congenital CMV is the commonest infective cause of microcephaly worldwide, ahead of toxoplasmosis and rubella, and is also the leading non-genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss. Most infected newborns are asymptomatic at birth yet can still develop late hearing loss, which is the argument for targeted newborn screening.

subject: OBGYN
q: A pregnant woman reports a mononucleosis-like illness after close contact with a toddler in daycare. The fetal scan shows microcephaly with periventricular calcifications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Wrong: toxoplasmosis gives scattered diffuse calcifications and follows cat or undercooked-meat exposure.
Correct: mononucleosis-like illness after toddler contact plus periventricular calcifications is congenital CMV.
Wrong: Zika gives cortical-subcortical calcifications and follows mosquito exposure.
Wrong: rubella gives cataract, heart defects and deafness, not this picture.
exp: Periventricular calcifications plus a mononucleosis-like maternal illness after contact with young children (CMV spreads in saliva and urine, and daycare toddlers are the classic source) point to congenital CMV. Toxoplasmosis classically causes scattered diffuse intracranial calcifications rather than a periventricular distribution.

subject: OBGYN
q: Which single history point most strongly raises suspicion of autosomal recessive primary microcephaly (MCPH) in a fetus with an isolated small head?
why: Wrong: advanced maternal age raises aneuploidy risk, not recessive disease.
Correct: consanguinity raises the chance of shared recessive alleles, the key clue to MCPH.
Wrong: a first pregnancy has no link to recessive microcephaly.
Wrong: gestational diabetes is linked to macrosomia and other anomalies, not primary microcephaly.
exp: Consanguinity is the key risk factor for autosomal recessive disease, and MCPH is a recessive group of disorders (MCPH1, ASPM and others). It is the question most often omitted from a fetal microcephaly workup and is especially relevant in Indian practice, where consanguineous marriage is common in several communities.

subject: OBGYN
q: Before labelling a fetus with a lagging head circumference as pathologically microcephalic, what is the single most important first step?
opts: Repeat the head-circumference scan only after delivery
Confirm gestational age against the first-trimester CRL-based dating scan
Proceed directly to amniocentesis without further scanning
why: Wrong: waiting until delivery abandons the antenatal diagnosis and delays counselling.
Correct: first-trimester CRL is the most accurate dating (±5–7 days) and must not be overridden by later biometry.
Wrong: empirical antibiotics have no role without an identified infection.
Wrong: invasive testing is premature before dates and the finding are confirmed.
exp: Wrong dates mimic a lagging parameter. First-trimester crown-rump length is the most accurate dating method (plus or minus 5-7 days); once dates are beyond the first trimester they should not be revised on later biometry, because doing so simply normalises genuine pathology.

subject: OBGYN
q: Standard estimated fetal weight formulas in routine obstetric ultrasound (for example Hadlock) combine which four biometric parameters?
