opts: BPD, HC, FL, amniotic fluid index
why: Correct: Hadlock EFW formulas use BPD, HC, AC and FL, with AC weighted most.
Wrong: cerebellar diameter is used for dating, not in standard EFW formulas.
Wrong: placental thickness is not part of EFW.
Wrong: AFI measures liquor volume, not fetal weight.
exp: Hadlock's estimated fetal weight formulas combine BPD, HC, AC and FL, with AC carrying the heaviest weight in most versions. Because AC dominates the estimate, a fetus with an isolated small head can still return a near-normal EFW, which is exactly why the individual parameters must be read separately rather than as a single weight.

subject: OBGYN
q: A term fetus has isolated microcephaly with normal AC and FL, reassuring umbilical and MCA Doppler, and no other structural anomaly on a detailed scan. What is the most appropriate obstetric plan?
opts: Immediate delivery regardless of cervical status, as for severe FGR
Standard term obstetric care while completing the infection and genetic workup and arranging neonatal counselling
Induction of labour only at 42 weeks, disregarding the head-circumference finding
why: Wrong: early delivery is for placental insufficiency (abnormal Doppler, growth arrest), absent here.
Correct: isolated microcephaly with normal growth and Doppler is a neurodevelopmental problem; continue term care with workup and counselling.
Wrong: no obstetric indication justifies iatrogenic prematurity.
Wrong: waiting to 42 weeks gives no benefit and ignores the finding.
exp: Early delivery in FGR is justified by evidence of placental insufficiency (abnormal Doppler, arrested growth), none of which is present here. An isolated small head is a neurological prognosis problem, not a placental one: the intervention belongs in the workup and in neonatal and family counselling, not in shortening the pregnancy.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a single episode of spotting. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows an endometrial thickness of 3 mm with a homogeneous endometrial echo. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Immediate hysteroscopic biopsy regardless of endometrial thickness
No tissue sampling needed now — endometrial thickness ≤4 mm has a very high negative predictive value for malignancy; reassure and biopsy only if bleeding recurs
Repeat ultrasonography in 6 months without any biopsy or follow-up plan
Start empirical progestin therapy without tissue diagnosis
why: Wrong — immediate invasive sampling is unnecessary when a thin stripe already has a very high negative predictive value
Correct — endometrial thickness ≤4 mm on TVS in postmenopausal bleeding has an NPV above 99% for cancer, so sampling is reserved for recurrent bleeding
Wrong — this gives no safety-net biopsy if bleeding recurs
Wrong — empirical hormones without tissue diagnosis can mask or delay a malignancy
exp: In postmenopausal bleeding, a transvaginal endometrial thickness ≤4 mm carries a negative predictive value >99% for endometrial cancer, so biopsy can reasonably be deferred if the stripe is thin and bleeding does not recur. Persistent or recurrent bleeding always mandates endometrial sampling regardless of thickness, since the cutoff reduces but does not eliminate risk.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 55-year-old woman presents with ascites, right-sided pleural effusion, and a solid ovarian mass on imaging. Both the ascites and pleural effusion resolve completely after the mass is surgically removed. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
why: Correct: Meigs syndrome is a benign fibroma with ascites and right pleural effusion that resolve after removal
Krukenberg tumour is a metastatic signet-ring tumour, usually from the stomach
OHSS follows ovulation induction, not a solid mass in a 55-year-old
Carcinomatosis means malignant spread, so fluid would not clear after removing the primary
exp: Meigs syndrome is the triad of a benign ovarian fibroma (or thecoma), ascites, and pleural effusion, classically right-sided, all of which resolve after resection of the tumour. This complete resolution after removal is the key feature distinguishing it from malignant ovarian tumours with peritoneal spread.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 28-year-old woman complains of a thin, greyish-white vaginal discharge with a fishy odour that worsens after intercourse. Vaginal pH is 5.5, and microscopy shows epithelial cells studded with bacteria obscuring the cell borders. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct: clue cells, pH over 4.5 and fishy odour meet Amsel criteria for bacterial vaginosis
Trichomonas gives frothy yellow-green discharge with motile flagellates and strawberry cervix
Candidiasis gives thick curdy discharge with itch and a normal acidic pH
Atrophic vaginitis affects oestrogen-deficient postmenopausal women
exp: Bacterial vaginosis is diagnosed using Amsel's criteria (at least 3 of 4): thin homogeneous discharge, vaginal pH greater than 4.5, a positive whiff (amine) test with KOH, and clue cells on microscopy, epithelial cells with a stippled, granular border from adherent coccobacilli, classically Gardnerella vaginalis.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 24-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset severe right iliac fossa pain, nausea, and vomiting for 6 hours. Pelvic ultrasound shows an enlarged right ovary (8 cm) with a whirlpool sign of the vascular pedicle on color Doppler and reduced venous flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Ruptured ectopic needs a positive pregnancy test and haemoperitoneum; it does not give a whirlpool sign
Correct: a twisted vascular pedicle (whirlpool sign) with reduced venous flow is diagnostic of torsion
Tubo-ovarian abscess presents with fever and a complex septic mass, not an acute whirlpool sign
OHSS follows ovulation induction and causes bilateral enlarged ovaries with ascites
exp: The whirlpool sign (a twisted, coiled vascular pedicle) with reduced or absent venous flow on color Doppler is the classic ultrasound finding of ovarian torsion, a surgical emergency treated by prompt laparoscopic detorsion to salvage the ovary. Because the ovary has a dual blood supply (ovarian and uterine arteries), arterial flow can persist despite torsion, so a normal arterial Doppler does not rule it out.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 22-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual cycles for 2 years, weight gain, and hirsutism. Pelvic ultrasound shows bilaterally enlarged ovaries with 14 peripheral follicles each measuring 4-8 mm, and serum testosterone is mildly elevated. Which diagnostic criteria is used to confirm the underlying diagnosis in this patient?
why: Correct: Rotterdam 2003 needs 2 of 3 (anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries) and fits this case
Amsterdam criteria are for Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)
NIH 1990 needs anovulation plus hyperandrogenism and ignores ovarian morphology; Rotterdam is the accepted standard
Bethesda system is for reporting cervical and thyroid cytology
exp: The Rotterdam 2003 criteria diagnose PCOS when at least 2 of 3 features are present: oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (classically 12 or more follicles of 2-9 mm or ovarian volume over 10 mL), after excluding mimics such as thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia, and non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

subject: OBGYN
q: A primigravida at 34 weeks presents with BP 168/112 mmHg, 3+ proteinuria, severe headache and brisk reflexes. Which drug should be started for seizure prophylaxis?
why: Phenytoin was inferior to magnesium sulphate in the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial
Diazepam was inferior to magnesium sulphate and sedates the newborn
Correct: magnesium sulphate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis (Magpie trial) and treatment of eclampsia
Levetiracetam has no established role in pre-eclampsia or eclampsia
exp: Magnesium sulphate is the drug of choice on two separate bodies of evidence: the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial established its superiority over phenytoin and diazepam for TREATING eclampsia, while the Magpie trial showed it roughly halves progression to eclampsia when used prophylactically. Monitor knee jerks, respiratory rate and urine output; calcium gluconate is the antidote.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman with known bronchial asthma has an atonic postpartum haemorrhage that has not responded to oxytocin and uterine massage. Which uterotonic must be avoided?
why: Correct: carboprost, a PGF2 alpha analogue, causes bronchoconstriction and is contraindicated in asthma
Misoprostol (a PGE1 analogue) is not barred by asthma
Methylergometrine is not barred by asthma; it is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia
Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic adjunct, not contraindicated in asthma
exp: Carboprost is a bronchoconstrictor and is contraindicated in asthma. Methylergometrine is instead contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia - knowing which uterotonic is barred by which comorbidity is the repeatedly tested point.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman with 7 weeks of amenorrhoea, a positive urine pregnancy test and right iliac fossa pain has an empty uterus with a right adnexal mass on scan. The commonest anatomical site for this pathology is:
why: The isthmus is the second commonest site
Correct: the ampulla holds about 70 percent of ectopic pregnancies
Ovarian pregnancy is rare, about 1-3 percent
Cervical pregnancy is rare, under 1 percent
exp: The ampulla accounts for roughly 70 percent of ectopic pregnancies, followed by the isthmus. Isthmic ectopics rupture earlier and more catastrophically because the isthmus is the narrowest and least distensible segment.

subject: OBGYN
q: A CTG in labour shows absent baseline variability with recurrent late decelerations and no accelerations. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
opts: Continue observation with repeat CTG in 30 minutes
Expedite delivery (emergency caesarean/instrumental) as this is a Category III tracing
Start oxytocin augmentation to shorten labour
why: Continued observation is inappropriate for a Category III tracing, which needs urgent action, not a repeat-and-wait approach.
Correct — absent variability plus recurrent late decelerations mandates prompt delivery.
Oxytocin augmentation would worsen uteroplacental perfusion in an already ominous tracing.
Amnioinfusion addresses cord-compression variable decelerations, not this pattern of uteroplacental insufficiency.
exp: A Category III CTG (absent variability with recurrent late decelerations, a sinusoidal pattern, or bradycardia) signals a high probability of fetal acidemia and mandates expedited delivery rather than continued observation or oxytocin augmentation — recognizing this NICHD three-tier classification (I reassuring, II indeterminate, III abnormal) is a frequently tested intrapartum fetal surveillance concept.

subject: OBGYN
q: The broad ligament, a double fold of peritoneum draping over the uterus, fallopian tubes and ovaries, is subdivided into three named parts. Which part specifically suspends the fallopian tube?
why: Mesometrium is the largest part, draping the uterine body below the tube/ovary attachment.
Mesovarium is the posterior fold suspending the ovary, not the tube.
The infundibulopelvic ligament is a separate lateral condensation carrying the ovarian vessels, not one of the three classic broad-ligament subdivisions.
Correct — the mesosalpinx is the superior part of the broad ligament enclosing and suspending the fallopian tube.
exp: The broad ligament has three named subdivisions: mesosalpinx (suspends the fallopian tube, superior-most), mesovarium (suspends the ovary posteriorly), and mesometrium (the bulk, below tube and ovary) — a frequently tested anatomy distinction, and the mesosalpinx is where paratubal (hydatid) cysts of Morgagni arise.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman with dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 32 weeks is being screened for oligohydramnios. Which method of amniotic fluid assessment is preferred in a twin gestation?
opts: Amniotic fluid index (AFI) summing all four quadrants across both sacs together
AFI measured using only the larger twin's sac
Umbilical artery Doppler resistance index alone, without fluid measurement
Single deepest vertical pocket (SDP) measured separately in each sac
why: AFI is a singleton-validated technique and quadrant summation across two sacs is not meaningful
assessing only one twin misses discordant fluid volume, a marker of TTTS or selective FGR
Doppler assesses perfusion, not liquor volume, and does not substitute for fluid assessment
correct - SDP per sac is the recommended twin-pregnancy method
exp: In twin pregnancy, amniotic fluid is assessed using the single deepest vertical pocket (SDP) measured separately in each sac, not the AFI used for singletons, because adjacent sacs compress each other's pockets and distort quadrant-based measurement.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 28-year-old with chronic hypertension conceives while taking enalapril and her BP remains well controlled on the same dose. What is the most appropriate step regarding her antihypertensive at this first antenatal visit?
opts: Continue enalapril unchanged for the rest of pregnancy since BP is controlled
Stop enalapril and switch to labetalol because of the risk of fetal renal dysgenesis and oligohydramnios
Switch her from enalapril to an angiotensin receptor blocker instead
Add hydrochlorothiazide to the existing enalapril rather than switching
why: good control does not offset the drug's teratogenic/fetotoxic class effect
correct - class switch is mandatory regardless of BP control
ARBs share the same fetotoxicity as ACE inhibitors
adding a diuretic does not address the fetotoxic drug that must be withdrawn
exp: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are fetotoxic in the second/third trimester, causing oligohydramnios, fetal renal dysgenesis, and skull ossification defects, so they must be stopped as soon as pregnancy is recognised and replaced with a pregnancy-safe agent such as labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa.

subject: OBGYN
q: Image described: pelvic ultrasound showing a solid right ovarian mass with a normal-appearing contralateral ovary. A 17-year-old girl with this mass has a markedly elevated serum LDH, and normal AFP and beta-hCG. Which ovarian tumour is most likely?
why: yolk sac tumour classically raises AFP, not LDH
immature teratoma is graded histologically and does not have a signature single marker
correct - LDH-secreting, AFP/hCG normal
choriocarcinoma would markedly raise beta-hCG
exp: Dysgerminoma is the commonest malignant germ cell tumour of the ovary in adolescents and young women, and its characteristic marker is raised LDH with normal AFP and beta-hCG, distinguishing it from yolk sac tumour (AFP) and choriocarcinoma (beta-hCG).

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman who conceived through IVF presents with lower abdominal pain at 6 weeks of gestation. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a live intrauterine pregnancy along with a separate adnexal mass and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Molar pregnancy with a coexistent live fetus
why: correct - IVF is the key risk-multiplier that should be flagged
a ruptured cyst does not typically produce a persistent separate adnexal mass with the IUP still visible
OHSS gives bilateral enlarged ovaries with ascites, not a discrete adnexal mass, and occurs earlier post-trigger
a coexistent mole with a live fetus is a distinct rare entity without this adnexal-mass picture
exp: Heterotopic pregnancy (simultaneous intrauterine and ectopic pregnancy) is rare spontaneously but its incidence rises sharply after assisted reproduction, so a live IUP with a coexisting adnexal mass and free fluid in an IVF pregnancy must be treated as heterotopic until excluded.

subject: OBGYN
q: Image described: wet mount microscopy shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast forms. A pregnant woman at 28 weeks complains of intense vulvar itching with thick, curd-like vaginal discharge, and the wet mount above is obtained. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days
why: oral fluconazole is generally avoided in pregnancy given the fetal-safety signal, though the risk at a single low dose is debated
correct - topical azole is the pregnancy-preferred route and duration
metronidazole treats bacterial vaginosis/trichomoniasis, not candidiasis, and would not clear pseudohyphae
clindamycin is a bacterial-vaginosis treatment, not an antifungal
exp: Vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy is treated with a topical azole (clotrimazole or miconazole) for 7 days rather than oral fluconazole, which carries a fetal-safety signal at higher or repeated doses in observational data.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman with known primary hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 50 mcg/day confirms pregnancy at 6 weeks gestation. What is the most appropriate management of her thyroid medication at this visit?
opts: Continue the same dose unchanged and recheck TSH only at term
Stop levothyroxine, since placental and fetal thyroid hormone production increases in pregnancy
Switch her from levothyroxine (T4) to liothyronine (T3) for better placental transfer
Increase the levothyroxine dose by roughly 25-30% and recheck TSH every 4 weeks
why: an unchanged dose risks maternal and fetal hypothyroidism through early pregnancy when demand is highest
thyroid hormone requirement increases, it does not fall, in pregnancy
T3 crosses the placenta poorly and is not standard therapy
correct - the standard empiric dose-increase and monitoring schedule
exp: Maternal levothyroxine requirement rises early in pregnancy due to increased thyroxine-binding globulin and first-trimester fetal dependence on maternal T4, so a pre-pregnancy dose should be empirically increased by about 25-30% with TSH checked every 4 weeks against trimester-specific targets.

subject: OBGYN
q: Image described: instrumental vaginal examination showing the fetal face with the mentum anterior, and the brow and orbits palpable through the introitus. A primigravida at full cervical dilatation needs an instrumental delivery for fetal distress and this presentation is found. Which instrument is contraindicated here?
opts: Either instrument may be safely used in this presentation
why: correct - vacuum is unsafe on a non-vertex (face) presentation
forceps can, in skilled hands, be used for a well-flexed mentoanterior face at outlet station
forceps can also be used at low station for mentoanterior face in skilled hands
the two instruments are not interchangeable given vacuum's contraindication
exp: Vacuum extraction requires traction on a well-flexed vertex and is contraindicated in face, brow, and other non-vertex presentations because the cup cannot achieve safe traction and risks fetal ocular/orbital injury; forceps remain an option for a well-flexed mentoanterior face in experienced hands.

subject: OBGYN
q: During assessment of pelvic organ support, a gynaecologist explains that division or stretching of one particular ligament complex during difficult childbirth or radical surgery is the key mechanism behind uterine and vault prolapse. Which structure provides the main lateral support to the uterus and cervix?
why: the round ligament maintains uterine anteversion, not vertical suspension
the uterosacral ligament contributes support but is not the main lateral suspensory structure
correct - the cardinal ligament is the principal level-I support
the broad ligament is a peritoneal fold, not a true supporting ligament
exp: The cardinal (transverse cervical, Mackenrodt's) ligament, running from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the pelvic side wall, is the principal structure suspending the uterus and cervix; its weakening or division is the chief mechanism of uterovaginal prolapse.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman who missed first-trimester aneuploidy screening presents at 16 weeks gestation requesting biochemical screening. Which combination of analytes constitutes the second-trimester quadruple marker test she should be offered?
opts: PAPP-A, free beta-hCG, nuchal translucency, and nasal bone assessment
AFP, hCG, and unconjugated estriol only (the triple test)
AFP, hCG, unconjugated estriol, and inhibin A
why: nuchal translucency and PAPP-A are first-trimester tools and are no longer valid at 16 weeks
this is the older triple test, now superseded by the quadruple test
correct - the quadruple marker panel
cfDNA is an option but is not the quadruple marker test being asked about
exp: The second-trimester quadruple marker test - maternal serum AFP, total/free-beta hCG, unconjugated estriol, and inhibin A, performed at 15-20 weeks - improves detection of Down syndrome and open neural tube defects over the older triple test by adding inhibin A.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman presents 4 days after an episode of unprotected intercourse requesting emergency contraception, and also wants a highly effective method of ongoing reversible contraception afterwards. What is the most appropriate single option to offer her?
opts: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg single oral dose
Combined oral pills using the Yuzpe regimen
why: correct - effective to day 5 and converts directly to ongoing contraception
oral levonorgestrel is licensed up to 72 hours and does not provide ongoing contraception
ulipristal is effective to 120 hours but is a one-time emergency pill, not ongoing contraception
the Yuzpe regimen is an older, less effective, higher-side-effect option than the copper IUCD here
exp: The copper IUCD is the most effective emergency contraceptive method, can be inserted up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse, and doubles as highly effective ongoing reversible contraception, making it the best choice when a woman needs both emergency cover and continued contraception.

subject: OBGYN
q: A postmenopausal woman aged 58 years presents with abdominal distension and early satiety. Examination reveals ascites and a fixed, irregular pelvic mass; CA-125 is markedly elevated. Image described: histopathology of the ovarian mass shows papillary fronds lined by atypical epithelium with concentric, calcified psammoma bodies. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: High-grade serous carcinoma of the ovary
why: mucinous cystadenocarcinoma shows glandular or cystic architecture with mucin-secreting epithelium, not papillary fronds with psammoma bodies
correct: papillary architecture with psammoma bodies in a postmenopausal woman with ascites and raised CA-125 is classic for high-grade serous carcinoma
granulosa cell tumour is a sex cord-stromal tumour with Call-Exner bodies and oestrogenic manifestations, a different histology and picture
Krukenberg tumour is a bilateral metastatic signet-ring cell tumour, typically from a gastric primary, not a primary papillary serous lesion
exp: High-grade serous carcinoma is the commonest and most lethal epithelial ovarian cancer, typically presenting late with ascites, an adnexal mass, and markedly elevated CA-125 in a postmenopausal woman; its hallmark histology is papillary architecture with psammoma bodies (concentric laminated calcifications). Most cases are now believed to arise from the fimbrial end of the fallopian tube rather than the ovarian surface epithelium, which has changed thinking on risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy in BRCA carriers.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 10 weeks by dates presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and hypovolaemic shock; ultrasound shows an empty uterine cavity with a gestational sac eccentrically located within the myometrium, lateral to the round ligament insertion. Which type of ectopic pregnancy is most consistent with this later presentation and catastrophic haemorrhage?
why: ampullary ectopic pregnancy is commonest overall but usually ruptures earlier, around 6-8 weeks, not with this later, myometrial presentation
isthmic ectopic pregnancy, in the narrow proximal tube, also tends to rupture early, around 6-8 weeks
ovarian ectopic pregnancy is rare and located within the ovary itself, not eccentrically within the myometrium near the cornu
correct: interstitial (cornual) ectopic pregnancies are more distensible and rupture later, around 9-12 weeks, with catastrophic haemorrhage
exp: Interstitial (cornual) ectopic pregnancies implant in the intramural, myometrium-surrounded segment of the tube, which is more distensible and vascular (supplied by both uterine and ovarian vessels) than the rest of the tube, allowing them to grow undetected until 9-12 weeks before rupturing catastrophically. This later, more severe presentation contrasts with the far more common ampullary ectopic, which typically ruptures earlier (6-8 weeks) owing to the thin ampullary wall.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 24-year-old woman presents with a small, painless vulval ulcer that healed spontaneously two weeks ago, now followed by unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy with matted nodes above and below the inguinal ligament. Image described: clinical photograph of grouped, tender inguinal and femoral lymph nodes separated by a linear depression along the inguinal ligament. Which organism is the most likely cause?
why: Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) causes a painful, ragged, soft ulcer with a painful suppurative bubo, not a painless self-healing ulcer with the groove sign
Treponema pallidum (primary syphilis) causes a painless, indurated, single chancre with firm non-suppurative nodes, not the groove sign
correct: the biphasic painless-ulcer-then-groove-sign presentation is classic for LGV due to Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3
Klebsiella granulomatis causes granuloma inguinale with beefy-red, friable, painless ulcers and pseudobuboes rather than true lymphadenopathy with a groove sign
exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3, classically produces a small, transient, often unnoticed primary ulcer followed weeks later by painful inguinal and femoral lymphadenopathy; when nodes on both sides of the inguinal (Poupart's) ligament enlarge, the intervening depression produces the pathognomonic groove sign. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice, and it remains an important cause of genital ulcer disease and its complications (strictures, elephantiasis) in tropical settings including India.

subject: OBGYN
q: A neonate develops respiratory distress and lethargy within 12 hours of birth. The mother had prolonged rupture of membranes (more than 18 hours) and was not screened or treated for group B Streptococcus colonization. Which measure, if given intrapartum, would most effectively have reduced this neonate's risk of early-onset sepsis?
opts: Intrapartum IV penicillin/ampicillin prophylaxis for GBS-colonized or high-risk mothers
Neonatal prophylactic oral antibiotics after birth
why: correct: intrapartum IV penicillin/ampicillin prophylaxis for GBS-colonized or risk-factor-positive mothers is the evidence-based intervention that reduces early-onset GBS sepsis
antenatal corticosteroids reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome from prematurity, not sepsis risk from GBS
maternal influenza vaccination protects against influenza-related complications, unrelated to GBS vertical transmission
oral antibiotics given to the neonate after birth do not prevent intrapartum vertical transmission that has already occurred
exp: Early-onset neonatal sepsis (within 72 hours of birth) is most often due to vertical transmission of group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) acquired during labour, with risk increased by prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever, and preterm labour. Universal antenatal GBS screening at 35-37 weeks (or a risk-based approach where screening is unavailable) followed by intrapartum intravenous penicillin or ampicillin prophylaxis for colonized or high-risk women is the standard strategy to prevent early-onset GBS disease.

subject: OBGYN
q: A primigravida is diagnosed as being in active labour and started on a partograph at 4 cm cervical dilation with regular painful contractions. Contemporary labour management guidance (ACOG's Safe Prevention of Primary Cesarean consensus, based on the Zhang labour curve) instead recommends that active labour, and hence a diagnosis of arrest of dilation, generally not be assessed until cervical dilation of at least:
why: 3 cm is within the latent phase by any definition and too early to diagnose active-phase arrest
4 cm was the traditional Friedman-curve threshold, now considered too early given contemporary labour curve data
correct: 6 cm is the revised threshold for active labour onset per ACOG's consensus based on the Zhang labour curve
8 cm is well into the active phase and not the threshold recommended for defining its onset
exp: Contemporary evidence (the Zhang curve) showed that cervical dilation from 4 to 6 cm proceeds far more slowly than classically taught by the Friedman curve, so applying the old 4 cm active-phase threshold led to many women being labelled as having arrested labour, and undergoing caesarean section, when they were simply still in a slow but normal latent phase. ACOG's 2014 Safe Prevention of the Primary Cesarean Delivery consensus therefore recommends that active labour be considered to begin at 6 cm, with arrest of the active phase only diagnosed beyond this point.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman on postpartum day 4 develops fever, right lower quadrant and flank pain, and a tender, cord-like mass extending from the pelvis toward the right upper abdomen. Image described: contrast CT shows a thrombosed tubular structure extending from the right adnexa cephalad, draining directly into a large central vein. This postpartum complication is more common on the right side because the right ovarian vein:
opts: Is shorter and drains into the left renal vein under higher pressure
Drains directly into the low-pressure inferior vena cava and crosses the ureter obliquely, predisposing to stasis and compression
Lacks valves entirely, unlike the left ovarian vein
Is compressed by the sigmoid colon during postpartum involution
why: this reverses the actual anatomy; it is the left ovarian vein, not the right, that drains into the left renal vein
correct: the right ovarian vein's direct, low-angle drainage into the IVC and its relationship to the ureter favour venous stasis and thrombosis on that side
both ovarian veins have valves, though valvular incompetence can occur on either side; complete absence of valves is not the explanation
the sigmoid colon lies on the left side of the pelvis and is not implicated in right ovarian vein compression
exp: Postpartum (puerperal) ovarian vein thrombophlebitis is more often right-sided because the right ovarian vein is longer, drains directly and somewhat obliquely into the inferior vena cava, and crosses the ureter, all of which favour venous stasis; the left ovarian vein, by contrast, drains into the left renal vein at a right angle with comparatively better flow. Dextrorotation of the enlarged puerperal uterus further compresses the right ovarian vein, compounding the stasis. It classically presents in the first postpartum week with fever and a tender abdominal mass, treated with anticoagulation and antibiotics.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 36-year-old woman at 12 weeks gestation wants definitive fetal karyotyping as early as possible after a high-risk first-trimester combined screening result. Image described: ultrasound-guided sampling of chorionic tissue from the placental edge is performed. Compared with amniocentesis performed at 16 weeks, this earlier test (chorionic villus sampling) carries which recognised limitation?
opts: It cannot be performed before 18 weeks gestation
It has a substantially higher overall miscarriage risk than amniocentesis
It cannot diagnose chromosomal aneuploidies at all
It cannot detect neural tube defects since amniotic fluid AFP is not sampled
why: CVS is specifically valued because it can be performed earlier, from about 10-13 weeks, not later than amniocentesis
with an experienced operator, CVS and amniocentesis carry comparable, low procedure-related miscarriage risks, not a substantially higher risk for CVS
CVS fully diagnoses chromosomal aneuploidies since chorionic villi share the fetal genotype; this is in fact its main indication
correct: CVS samples no amniotic fluid, so it cannot measure amniotic AFP or acetylcholinesterase and therefore cannot screen for open neural tube defects
exp: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS), performed at 10-13 weeks by sampling placental (chorionic) tissue, allows earlier definitive karyotyping than amniocentesis (usually done at 15-20 weeks) but samples no amniotic fluid, so it cannot measure amniotic AFP or acetylcholinesterase and therefore cannot screen for open neural tube defects; a woman undergoing CVS still needs a second-trimester maternal serum AFP or detailed anomaly scan for that purpose. CVS also carries a small but real risk of confined placental mosaicism, which can complicate result interpretation.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman with an uncomplicated, normotensive pregnancy and delivery develops severe headache, blurred vision, and a blood pressure of 168/112 mmHg on postpartum day 5, after being discharged home normotensive. Which statement about this presentation is correct?
opts: Preeclampsia cannot occur after delivery, so an alternative diagnosis such as migraine should be sought first
New-onset postpartum preeclampsia can occur up to 6 weeks after delivery even without antenatal hypertension, and requires the same urgent evaluation and treatment as antepartum disease
Since the antenatal course was normotensive, magnesium sulphate is not indicated even if she develops seizures
This presentation is expected postpartum physiology and needs only outpatient follow-up
why: postpartum preeclampsia is a well-recognised, distinct clinical entity and must be actively considered, not dismissed in favour of migraine
correct: postpartum preeclampsia can occur de novo up to 6 weeks after delivery and warrants the same urgent evaluation and treatment as antepartum disease
magnesium sulphate remains indicated for seizure prophylaxis or treatment in postpartum preeclampsia with severe features or eclampsia, regardless of the antenatal course
severe hypertension with headache and visual symptoms postpartum is not normal physiology and needs urgent, not merely outpatient, evaluation
exp: Preeclampsia (and eclampsia) can present for the first time in the postpartum period, most often within the first 48 hours but occasionally up to 6 weeks after delivery, even in women who were entirely normotensive throughout pregnancy and labour. New-onset postpartum hypertension with severe features (BP 160/110 or higher, headache, visual disturbance) requires the same urgent evaluation and treatment as antepartum severe preeclampsia, including magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis, and clinicians must counsel women to seek care for these red-flag symptoms after discharge.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 24-year-old woman underwent suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole 2 weeks ago; histopathology confirmed the diagnosis and her serum beta-hCG is declining appropriately. What is the recommended follow-up protocol to detect persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia?
opts: Weekly serum beta-hCG until 3 consecutive normal values, then monthly for 6 months, with reliable contraception throughout surveillance
A single beta-hCG check at 6 weeks post-evacuation, with no further follow-up if normal
Routine pelvic ultrasound every 2 weeks for 6 months, without serial hCG monitoring
Chest X-ray monthly for 1 year as the sole surveillance tool, hCG monitoring not required
why: correct, standard post-molar surveillance protocol
a single check misses the 15-20% who develop persistent GTN, which usually shows up over weeks to months
imaging cannot substitute for the hCG trend, the sensitive marker of trophoblastic activity
chest imaging is used only if metastatic GTN is suspected, not as primary surveillance, and pregnancy must be avoided throughout follow-up
exp: After molar evacuation, about 15-20% of complete moles develop persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, so surveillance relies on serial beta-hCG rather than imaging alone. Weekly hCG is checked until three consecutive normal values, then monthly for a further 6 months, and the patient must use reliable contraception throughout so a new pregnancy does not confound the hCG trend. A rising or plateauing hCG during this period triggers staging and chemotherapy work-up for GTN.

subject: OBGYN
q: A woman at 9 weeks of gestation is diagnosed with a missed abortion (absent fetal cardiac activity, closed cervical os) on ultrasound and chooses medical management instead of surgical evacuation. Which regimen is most appropriate as per current recommendations?
opts: Misoprostol 400 mcg as a single sublingual dose, with no mifepristone
Mifepristone 200 mg orally, followed 24-48 hours later by misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally or buccally
High-dose intravenous oxytocin infusion alone until expulsion
Medical management is contraindicated in missed abortion; surgical evacuation is mandatory
why: misoprostol alone is less effective than the combined regimen and is reserved for settings where mifepristone is unavailable
correct, priming with mifepristone before misoprostol gives significantly higher complete expulsion rates
oxytocin is ineffective for early first-trimester evacuation as the uterus has few oxytocin receptors at this gestation
medical management is an accepted, safe alternative to surgical evacuation in a haemodynamically stable woman
exp: For first-trimester missed abortion, combining mifepristone (an antiprogestin that primes the myometrium and cervix) with misoprostol given 24-48 hours later achieves substantially higher complete-expulsion rates than misoprostol alone. This combined regimen is now the WHO/FOGSI-preferred medical approach where mifepristone is available, reserving misoprostol-only protocols for settings without access to mifepristone. Surgical evacuation remains an option but is not mandatory in a stable patient who prefers medical management.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 28-year-old woman presents with continuous, painless leakage of urine per vaginum 10 days after a caesarean section performed for prolonged obstructed labour. To differentiate a vesicovaginal fistula from a ureterovaginal fistula at the bedside, which test is most useful?
opts: Three-swab (dye) test with intravesical instillation of methylene blue
Pelvic examination under anaesthesia without any dye instillation
why: renal function tests do not localize the site of leakage
a urine culture identifies infection, not the anatomical source of continuous leakage
correct, staining pattern of the three swabs localizes a vesicovaginal versus ureterovaginal fistula
examination without dye cannot distinguish a small fistula tract from normal vaginal wall
exp: The three-swab test remains a simple bedside method to localize a urinary fistula after obstructed labour or pelvic surgery: methylene blue is instilled into the bladder and three vaginal swabs are placed at different depths. Staining of the swab closest to the introitus confirms a vesicovaginal fistula, while a swab that is wet with clear, unstained urine suggests a ureterovaginal fistula requiring IV indigo carmine or CT urography for confirmation. Obstructed labour remains the leading cause of urogenital fistula in low-resource settings in India.

subject: OBGYN
q: A 26-year-old woman with well-controlled epilepsy on sodium valproate monotherapy is planning conception. What is the most appropriate change to her management before she conceives?
opts: Continue valproate unchanged, since switching antiepileptics before pregnancy increases the risk of breakthrough seizures
Stop all antiepileptic medication for the duration of pregnancy to avoid any fetal drug exposure
Add phenytoin as add-on therapy to allow a lower valproate dose
Switch to a lower-risk antiepileptic such as levetiracetam or lamotrigine and start high-dose folic acid supplementation preconceptionally
why: valproate has the highest teratogenic risk among antiepileptics and should be avoided when an alternative is feasible
abruptly stopping risks maternal seizures and status epilepticus
adding phenytoin increases polytherapy teratogenic risk rather than reducing it
correct, preconceptional switch to a lower-risk agent plus high-dose folic acid is the recommended strategy
exp: Sodium valproate carries the highest risk of major congenital malformations (especially neural tube defects) and dose-dependent neurodevelopmental impairment among antiepileptic drugs, so guidelines recommend switching to a lower-risk agent such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam whenever seizure control can be maintained. Any switch should be done preconceptionally and gradually, never abruptly, to avoid breakthrough seizures, and high-dose folic acid is started before conception. Stopping treatment outright risks maternal seizures and status epilepticus, which are themselves dangerous to mother and fetus.
